sources.news_title: ICE to require body cameras during vehicle stops after fatal encounters
sources.text:
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) will require its officers to utilize body-worn cameras during vehicle stops, a top administration official said Sunday, following a pair of recent fatal shootings by federal agents that have intensified scrutiny of the agency’s enforcement tactics.
Tom Homan, the Trump administration’s border czar, spoke about the directive during an appearance on Fox News' Fox & Friends, stating that ICE leadership has ordered at least one officer to record video during traffic operations as the agency accelerates a nationwide rollout of the technology.
The policy shift follows the fatal shootings of a Colombian delivery driver in Biddeford, Maine, on July 13, and a Mexican national in Houston on July 7. Neither incident was captured on body camera, fueling public protests and demands for greater transparency amid the administration's broader mass deportation campaign.
"The director of ICE put out instructions that whenever possible, that at least one body camera be worn," Homan said, arguing that the technology primarily protects law enforcement. "They exonerate more law enforcement than they convict, and I want officers wear body cameras because I want the American people see what the officer saw when they took that action."
Expansion Amid Mounting Scrutiny
The recent fatalities are part of a broader rise in lethal encounters involving federal immigration authorities. At least six people have been killed during ICE enforcement actions since January 2025, according to data tracked by Newsweek.
The lack of video evidence from the Texas and Maine encounters quickly turned the agency's camera policies into a central point of contention. While ICE initially suspended most vehicle stops to review its safety procedures following the shootings, President Donald Trump quickly ordered agents to resume the practice, calling traffic stops a vital enforcement tool.
According to Homan, who also appeared on CBS News' Face the Nation on Sunday, the cameras have already been purchased, and personnel training is underway for a comprehensive nationwide deployment. He contended that body-worn cameras offer a definitive perspective that bystander or surveillance footage cannot replicate.
"You can have something with a cell phone camera across the street," Homan said on Fox & Friends. "You can have city cameras that they can show you different things, but nothing's going to match what the officer saw just before he took that action."
ICE originally launched a pilot program for body-worn cameras in 2024, deploying them to select teams in Baltimore, Buffalo, Detroit, Philadelphia, and Washington, D.C. However, a wider expansion had previously stalled due to federal funding disputes and partisan gridlock over immigration enforcement resources.
A Timeline of Fatal Federal Agent-Related Shootings
March 15, 2025
Location: South Padre Island, Texas
Martinez was shot by an ICE Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) officer after what ICE described as a failure to follow law enforcement instructions during a traffic incident as agents worked with local police on immigration enforcement. Initial reports did not reveal the agency's involvement, with the details coming to light through internal ICE records.
December 31, 2025
Keith Porter Jr., 43
Location: Los Angeles
Porter was fatally shot by an off-duty ICE officer on New Year’s Eve. Local reports said Porter was firing a gun into the air in celebration of the holiday. The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) told Newsweek at the time that an off-duty ICE officer responded to an "active shooter situation" at his apartment complex. DHS told ABC7 Los Angeles that the off-duty officer ordered Porter to put down the weapon, and the officer fired his weapon when Porter did not comply. The agency also claimed that Porter fired three rounds at the officer before he died.
January 7, 2026
Location: Minneapolis
ICE has said that Renee, a writer and mother of three, was fatally shot after purposefully driving her car at ICE agents. However, witnesses and Minneapolis Mayor Jacob Frey refuted these claims. Then-DHS Secretary Kristi Noem said Renee was perpetrating “an act of domestic terrorism” and ICE agents acted in self-defense.
January 24, 2026
Alex Pretti, 37
Location: Minneapolis
Pretti, an intensive care nurse, died on the streets of Minneapolis after a confrontation with federal agents. One of several videos taken of the incident shows Pretti holding a cellphone in his right hand before a struggle with the agents, with one later seen stepping away holding a handgun that appeared to be removed from his waistband, followed by gunfire. Minneapolis Police Chief Brian O’Hara said he saw no evidence that Pretti brandished a weapon and described him as appearing to lawfully record while legally carrying.
July 7, 2026
Location: Houston
The DHS recently told Newsweek that Araujo, a Mexican national, had died from his injuries in hospital after he was shot by a federal agent. ICE agents had been trying to arrest Araujo, but he had attempted to evade officers, a DHS spokesperson said.
"From information we are receiving, he rammed an ICE law enforcement vehicle, refused to follow multiple verbal commands, and weaponized his vehicle in an attempt to run over an ICE law enforcement officer resulting in our officer firing his weapon in self-defense," a spokesperson told Newsweek, adding that the FBI was investigating the incident.
July 13, 2026
Joan Sebastian Durán Guerrero, 25
Location: Biddeford, Maine
An ICE officer fired his weapon “fearing for public safety” as Guerrero, in a vehicle, “attempted to flee the scene,” the DHS said in a statement. He was not the target of the enforcement operation. The married father of a 3-year-old daughter was legally authorized to work in the United States, according to government officials, the Maine Immigrants' Rights Coalition, and Presente! Maine.
FBI Will Continue Investigating ICE Encounters
Separately on Sunday, the Department of Justice (DOJ) and the DHS pushed back against reports suggesting the FBI would no longer investigate violent confrontations involving ICE personnel.
In a joint statement emailed to Newsweek, the agencies said claims of a policy change were "false" and emphasized that the relationship between DHS and DOJ regarding investigations of assaults on federal officers "has not changed." The statement added that the FBI "will continue to investigate in accordance with agency policy."
The agencies also stressed that the Trump administration remains committed to prosecuting attacks on law enforcement personnel. "This administration has been clear, anyone who assaults law enforcement will be prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law," the statement said.
DOJ and DHS described themselves as partners in "addressing crime and upholding the rule of law, while securing the safety and security of American communities."
Contact Newsweek editor for this story: Steve Mollman and Anthony Murray.

sources.news_title: ICE will require its officers to record vehicle stops
sources.text:
ICE will require its officers to record vehicle stops
Loading...
In the wake of multiple fatal shootings involving U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers, the agency will require its officers to record vehicle stops with at least one body camera, Trump administration border czar Tom Homan said Sunday.
“They exonerate more law enforcement than they convict, and I want officers to wear body cameras because I want the American people to see what the officers saw when they took that action,” Mr. Homan said on the “Fox & Friends Weekend” program.
Mr. Homan’s comments come after federal immigration agents fatally shot two men six days apart during traffic stops in Texas and Maine earlier this month. There is no body-camera footage from ICE agents involved in those incidents.
In a separate interview on CBS’ “Face the Nation” show, Mr. Homan said money for the cameras was held up during the partial government shutdown earlier this year.
“The cameras have been purchased right now,” Mr. Homan said. “They’re training the trainer in deploying the cameras nationwide.”
Traffic stops resume
The agency’s tactics came under renewed public scrutiny in recent days after an ICE officer on July 13 killed a driver from Colombia in the coastal Maine town of Biddeford, about 15 miles south of Portland. Six days earlier, another ICE officer in Houston fatally shot a Mexican national.
Mr. Homan said last week the agency would temporarily suspend most vehicle stops around the country to review procedures. Within 24 hours of Mr. Homan’s comments, U.S. President Donald Trump directed federal immigration agents to resume them.
The back-to-back shootings sparked protests in Maine, Houston, and Boston and raised questions over ICE agents’ lack of body cameras.
ICE launched a body-camera pilot program in 2024 and deployed cameras to officers in five cities: Baltimore, Buffalo, Detroit, Philadelphia, and Washington, D.C.
The Trump administration moved last year to slow-walk the program, urging Congress to cut funding by 75%, Reuters reported in January.
In February, after the killing of two U.S. citizens during an immigration crackdown in Minnesota, then U.S. Department of Homeland Security chief Kristi Noem said the body camera program would be rolled out to ICE agents nationwide “as funding is available.”
At least seven people have been shot dead during federal immigration enforcement operations since January 2025, when Trump launched mass deportations after returning to office following campaign promises of an immigration crackdown.
(Reporting by Diana Novak Jones; Editing by Sergio Non and Chizu Nomiyama )

sources.news_title: ICE required to wear body cams for most traffic stops after fatal shootings
sources.text:
ICE now required to wear body cameras for most traffic stops after fatal shootings, Trump’s border czar says
Trump administration has blamed Democrat-led government shutdowns for delays in federal agents wearing body cams
Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents will be required to wear at least one body camera during most traffic stops, according to the Trump administration’s border czar, after ICE officers without cameras fatally shot two people in the span of a week this month.
Agents will be required to use the body-worn cameras “whenever possible,” White House border czar Tom Homan said in an interview on Fox & Friends on Sunday.
“I’m a big proponent of body cams, always have been,” Homan said.
“They exonerate more law enforcement than they convict, and I want officers to wear body cameras because I want the American people to see what the officer saw when they took that action.”
In a separate interview on Sunday with Face the Nation on CBS News, Homan blamed recent Democrat-led government shutdowns for delaying the rollout of ICE body cameras.
“Everybody in ICE would have a camera now if the government wasn’t shut down by Democratic members of Congress,” said Homan, adding that cameras are being purchased and deployed now, while officers are being trained on how to incorporate the cameras into operations.
ICE told The Independent earlier this week that more than half of its field offices already have body cameras deployed, with the remaining offices set to receive the cameras within the next 60 days.
The new requirement comes after ICE agents without cameras fatally shot two men during vehicle stops in Houston, Texas and Maine within one week.
Those men were not the intended target of immigration enforcement operations, prompting widespread protests and calls for accountability.
Critics of the Trump administration argue such cameras are necessary, given that White House officials have often made misleading claims about the facts of high-profile incidents involving Department of Homeland Security officers using lethal force.
“Even if the government is telling the truth, however, most Americans no longer give the Trump administration the benefit of the doubt,”The Washington Post’s editorial board wrote Monday. “DHS has made these situations more combustible by squandering credibility in previous cases when force was used.”
At the beginning of this year, after immigration agents carried out a pair of fatal shootings against protesters in Minnesota, then-Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem vowed that agents nationwide would soon be equipped with body-worn cameras, and the agency was awarded an additional $20 million in April to aid in getting cameras into the field.
Even with a change in body camera policy, ICE continues to face scrutiny over the shootings in Texas and Maine.
The brother of Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, the 52-year-old Mexican national who was fatally shot by an ICE agent in Houston, claims they were unaware that the unmarked cars following them were federal agents. Homan told Face the Nation he had not seen video evidence that the officers turned on their emergency lights in the operation.
In Monday’s shooting in Biddeford, Maine, in which an ICE agent killed Joan Sebastian Guerrero, a 26-year-old father with work authorization, a witness told Reuters he heard the victim tell law enforcement, “I tried to stop.”
An ex-wife of the agent accused of committing the Maine shooting told The Independent she had long worried about his temperament, but ICE failed to properly vet him.
“For years, I told people he was going to hurt somebody,” she told The Independent.
ICE appeared to suggest that The Independent’s reporting on that subject was an attempt to “dox our law enforcement officers” and did not respond directly to the claims.
The shootings briefly prompted a pause in ICE vehicle stops, though President Donald Trump ordered agents to resume the stops on Wednesday, calling them one of the agency’s “most important and effective Crime Fighting tools” in a social media post.

US Immigration and Customs Enforcement will require body cameras during vehicle stops after recent fatal shootings involving officers. The decision follows public backlash and is part of a body-camera program initiated in 2024 but previously delayed due to budget constraints during a government shutdown.

In response to a series of fatal shootings involving U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers, the agency is set to mandate body cameras for its officers during vehicle stops, according to a statement by Tom Homan, a border czar from the Trump administration, on Sunday.
Homan’s comments came amid public outrage following the deaths of two men in separate traffic stops in Texas and Maine earlier this month. Criticism heightened due to the absence of body-camera footage from these incidents despite a pilot program initiated in 2024.

sources.news_title: Trump border czar says "I think body cameras are the way to go" after deadly ICE shootings
sources.text:
Trump border czar says "I think body cameras are the way to go" after deadly ICE shootings
White House border czar Tom Homan said on Sunday, "I think body cameras are the way to go," after fatal shootings by federal officers in Texas and Maine earlier this month.
"I think body cameras let the American people know what that officer sees when he takes that action," Homan said on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan."
On July 7, an Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer shot and killed a Mexican national in Houston who had lived in the U.S. for decades. Days later, an ICE officer shot and killed a Colombian man in Biddeford, Maine. In both cases, the immigration personnel involved in the shootings were not wearing body cameras.
Homan said Sunday that "you can have a cellphone camera from a witness on the side, you can have, you know, city cameras or whatever. But I want the American people to see what that officer sees when he makes the decision and takes an action."
"I think the American people need to see what that officer sees and hears," Homan added. "I think it's important."
Homan has previously advocated for body cameras. And last week, the Department of Homeland Security announced that every Immigration and Customs Enforcement arrest team will have at least one officer equipped with a camera going forward. DHS said shortly after the Houston shooting that body cameras had been deployed to more than half of ICE's field offices, with the remaining offices set to receive them within 60 days.
The body cameras issue was part of negotiations between Senate Democrats and Republicans during a shutdown of the Department of Homeland Security earlier this year. At the time, Democrats refused to fund the department as they sought reforms to the administration's immigration enforcement operation following two deadly shootings by federal agents in Minneapolis in January.
During the negotiations over immigration enforcement, the Trump administration signaled openness to expanding the use of body cameras. But negotiations ultimately fell apart. Democrats eventually opted to approve funding for the rest of the department in April, which included $20 million for body cameras, while Republicans later approved a roughly $70 billion package unilaterally to fund Immigration and Customs Enforcement and Border Patrol through the end of the Trump administration.
Homan on Sunday pointed to the DHS shutdown, claiming, "Everybody in ICE would have a camera now if the government wasn't shut down by Democratic members of Congress."
"There was money in that bill that they held up," he said. "But because the government shut down, we're behind on that."
Democratic lawmakers have criticized DHS's slow rollout of body cameras, given the funding approved in April, along with the "big, beautiful bill" passed last year. But Homan said the $20 million the department received earlier this year "wasn't enough."
"It didn't fund everything, but now we have the funding after reconciliation," Homan said, referring to the $70 billion package passed in June. "The cameras have been purchased, right now they're training the trainer in deploying the cameras nationwide."
The shootings in Texas and Maine have drawn renewed scrutiny on ICE's practices. Homan said "we got to let the investigations play out," but he noted that DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin "took some action in concern of the safety of the agents and how we do operations" with a pause on vehicle stops. President Trump overturned that suspension on Wednesday. Both men were shot during attempted vehicle stops, and DHS has acknowledged that they were not the intended targets of the immigration operations.
Homan said more broadly, he's concerned about rhetoric, pointing to statements, including from members of Congress, encouraging people to resist Immigration and Customs Enforcement. He said "I actually think that emboldens some people to say, 'I'm not going to comply with ICE.'"
"And I think no matter what people think of ICE, no matter what you think of immigration law, you should always comply with law enforcement," Homan said.
Homan said even unmarked law enforcement vehicles are equipped with emergency lights and sirens, along with an insignia worn by officers, that he argued would make clear that they're law enforcement. In the Maine and Texas cases, Homan said he didn't know whether those lights were used.
"I'm saying our vehicles are equipped with emergency lights," Homan said. "If they didn't activate the lights, then there's an issue there."
